lesson.menu_title: Future Forms -- Plans, Predictions and the First Ninety Days
lesson.menu_desc: Answer the plan question in a senior interview: will decides, going to reports a decision already made, and the present continuous states what is already in the calendar -- 34 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 14 -- Future Forms for Plans and Predictions
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Lucia Nishiyama Serra | Lesson 14 -- Future Forms for Plans and Predictions
lesson.grammar_point: future forms (will, going to, present continuous)

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: the direction and the speed something is moving over time
to retire an old system gradually, on a planned date
a small result you can deliver fast, to build trust early
the regular rhythm of meetings or reports
to plan something in detail, step by step, before you start
a force that makes progress slower and harder
to say what you expect to happen, based on data you already have
the first measurement, used later to show how much changed

paras: Near the end of every senior interview there is a question about the future. What would your first ninety days look like? Where do you see this program in a year? Candidates who are strong everywhere else often lose the room here, and the reason is not the plan. It is the grammar. They put the entire answer in one form, usually will, and to an American listener that sounds like a plan invented during the interview. English has three common ways of pointing at the future, and each one tells the listener something different about how solid the plan already is.

The first is will. You use it when you decide as you speak, when you predict, and when you promise: I will take a baseline in week one, so we can measure the change. The second is be going to. It reports a decision that existed before this conversation started, or a prediction you can already see in the evidence: I am going to map out the first ninety days this weekend. Hiring is going to be our biggest headwind. The third is the present continuous, and it is the strongest of all in an interview, because it means the thing is already arranged, with a time and usually with other people: I am presenting the plan to the board on Tuesday. There is also the present simple, but it belongs to timetables that nobody controls: the onboarding week starts on the sixth of January.

Two traps catch almost every Brazilian speaker. The first is marking the future twice. After when, as soon as, before, after and until, English puts the future in only one half of the sentence: As soon as the trajectory is clear, I will move to a two-week cadence. Never as soon as the trajectory will be clear. The second is the small word to. Will is a modal, and no modal accepts to: I will map out the plan, never I will to map out the plan. Get those two right and mix the three forms on purpose, and the interviewer stops hearing a wish and starts hearing a plan.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B1 reading, adapted from an executive interview guide

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: The three future forms are not interchangeable: will decides or predicts, going to reports a decision already made, and the present continuous states a fixed arrangement.
In an interview you should answer every question about the future with will, because it is the safest and most formal form.
After when and as soon as, English marks the future twice, once in each half of the sentence.

gapfill.text: will = you decide as you speak, you predict, you promise. be going to = the decision was already made, or the evidence is in front of you. Present continuous = a fixed arrangement with a time and other people. After when, as soon as, before and until, use the present -- never will.

bank.label: Useful sentences for a plan question
items: In week one I will take a baseline, so we can measure the change.
I am going to map out the first ninety days before I start.
I am presenting the plan to the board on Tuesday.
Hiring is going to be our biggest headwind next year.
We are sunsetting the legacy platform in March.
As soon as the trajectory is clear, I will move to a two-week cadence.
I am going to look for one quick win in the first month.
I will forecast the savings before the budget meeting.

forms.title: Five moves with the future
cards: "I will take a baseline in week one." No to after will, and the verb never changes: will take, will move, will forecast.
am / is / are going to + verb
"I am going to map out the first ninety days." Also for a prediction the evidence already shows: "Look at the trajectory -- hiring is going to be the headwind."
"I am presenting the plan to the board on Tuesday." There is a time, and usually other people are already in that calendar.
"The onboarding week starts on the sixth of January." Programs, flights and calendars that nobody controls take the simple form.
no will in the time clause
"As soon as the trajectory is clear, I will move to a two-week cadence." The same after when, before, after and until.

items.situation: A recruiter asks what your first month in the role would look like. Answer in one sentence with something you have already decided.
tips: I am going to map out the first thirty days before I start.
I am going to spend the first two weeks with the engineering leads.

items.situation: The interviewer asks what is already in your calendar next week. Answer with the arrangement.
tips: I am presenting the plan to the steering group on Tuesday.
I am meeting two of the platform leads on Thursday.

items.situation: You are asked what will be hardest about the plan. Give a prediction with the evidence behind it.
tips: Hiring is going to be our biggest headwind.
Looking at the cost trajectory, the second quarter will be the tight one.

items.situation: A board member asks when you will commit to a reporting rhythm. Use a time clause.
tips: As soon as the baseline is ready, I will move to a two-week cadence.
When the migration is stable, I will commit to a date.

items.situation: Someone asks what happens to the old system. Answer with the decision and the date.
tips: We are sunsetting it in March.
We are going to sunset it after the migration, and the date is already in the plan.

items: Round 1 -- Guided
In three sentences, describe your first month in a new role: one with going to, one with the present continuous and a date, and one prediction with will.
Round 2 -- The one-minute plan
Give a one-minute ninety-day plan for a real role: what you will measure first, what you have already decided, what is already booked, and what you predict.
Round 3 -- Under pressure
Deliver the same plan in thirty seconds, and add one sentence starting with As soon as.
Curveball
The interviewer asks "And what will you do if hiring is slower than you expect?" Answer with one prediction and one decision you have already made.

answerkey.title: Reveal the model ninety-day answer
list: Model: "In week one I will take a baseline, so that in ninety days we can both see exactly what moved. I am going to map out the first thirty days before I start, and I am meeting the engineering leads on Thursday, so the plan will not be written in a vacuum. Hiring is going to be our biggest headwind -- the cost trajectory already says so, and I would rather forecast that now than explain it in June. We are sunsetting the legacy platform in March. As soon as the migration is stable, I will move the team to a two-week reporting cadence and look for one quick win the board can see."
Already decided (going to): I am going to map out the first thirty days before I start.
Already booked (present continuous): I am meeting the engineering leads on Thursday. / We are sunsetting the legacy platform in March.
Prediction (will / going to): Hiring is going to be our biggest headwind next year.
Promise decided as you speak (will): In week one I will take a baseline.
Time clause, no will: As soon as the migration is stable, I will move to a two-week cadence.
answerkey.note: will = decided now, predicted, promised. going to = decided before. Present continuous = already in the calendar. Present simple = a timetable. After when, as soon as, before and until, the future is marked only once.

listenings.text: I run about forty senior interviews a year, and the plan question is where I learn the most. Here is what I hear from a weak candidate. The whole answer comes back in will. I will meet the team, I will review the roadmap, I will build a plan. Every sentence is correct English, and the whole thing still sounds like it was invented in the last ninety seconds, because will is the form you use when you decide while you are speaking. Now here is the strong version. Some of it comes back as going to, which tells me the decision existed before I asked the question. I am going to spend the first two weeks with the engineering leads. Some of it comes back in the present continuous, with a date attached, which tells me it is already arranged and other people are already holding that time. And somewhere in the middle, the candidate names the headwind. That is the one thing I ask everybody for. Tell me what is going to make this plan harder, and tell me before I have to ask.

Hi, this is the short version of the January plan, so you do not have to read the whole deck. First, the calendar. I am presenting the plan to the steering group on the fourteenth of January, and that meeting is already booked, so please send me your numbers before the tenth. Second, the decision we have already made. We are going to sunset the legacy platform, and the date is March. That is not a proposal any more, it is in the plan, so please stop building new reports on top of it. Third, the part I am not committing to yet. I want a two-week reporting cadence, and I know some of you want it tomorrow, but I will only commit to it once the baseline exists. Take the baseline in week one, and as soon as I can see the trajectory, I will confirm the rhythm. Last thing. My honest forecast is that hiring is going to be our biggest headwind this year, so if you can pull one quick win forward into February, do it.
